edges.limitations: The coat has never been examined in human hair cells, in a patient or otherwise, so the identity of the human structure with the mouse one is assumed from protein orthology. edges.description: The full time course - normal development, then progressive loss of stereocilia and bundle coherence from six weeks - was established in this line, together with the negative controls that rule out an attachment-crown or transduction mechanism.
edges.limitations: The background carries Cdh23ahl, the age-related hearing loss allele of C57BL/6, which is a confound for any age-dependent cochlear phenotype; the first study addressed it by comparing littermates rather than by moving the allele off the background. Bundle damage was scored by counting missing stereocilia on scanning electron microscopy in small numbers of cochleae. And no human bundle has been examined, so the correspondence to the human disease is inferred entirely from the shared gene.

edges.description: The noise arm. Six-week-old mutants and littermate controls received the same two-hour 94 dB SPL bandpass exposure; controls recovered to baseline by two weeks and mutants did not, at two weeks or at eight.
edges.limitations: Fidelity is UNKNOWN, not LOW, and the distinction is deliberate: the experiment is well controlled and the result is clear, but there is no human observation of any kind to compare it against, so how faithfully it represents a human patient cannot be assessed. Two further limits belong on the result itself. Threshold shifts were measured against an 80 dB SPL ceiling, and the mutants' baseline high-frequency thresholds already sit near that ceiling, so the measured shift understates the damage at exactly the frequencies where the disease is worst. And the exposure paradigm is a single laboratory dose, not the chronic, variable noise history a person accumulates.

edges.description: The model produces sensorineural hearing loss of cochlear origin, which is the human endpoint, but on a different schedule. Mouse hearing is normal at first and then declines from about three weeks at high frequencies, spreading to lower ones with age. Human hearing loss is present at birth or within months and then worsens only slowly.
edges.limitations: The onset divergence is the substantive limitation and is the subject of an open human-model mismatch discussion. There is a second, quieter one: the two studies of this same line disagree in degree, the later one finding threshold elevations less pronounced and slower to spread than the earlier, which the authors attribute to the recordings being made in different institutions. Any quantitative claim taken from this model should carry that.

edges.description: Auditory function is impaired, establishing that the gene's role in hearing is conserved across vertebrates, and the early onset is the closer match to the human congenital presentation.
edges.limitations: Fidelity is LOW for structural reasons rather than experimental ones. Zebrafish have no cochlea, no outer hair cells and no tectorial membrane, so nothing in this model can speak to the amplification and bundle-maintenance mechanism the mouse establishes; the readout is a behavioural startle response, not an audiogram. Two paralogues had to be removed together, which has no human counterpart. And the resemblance of its time course to the human one is a resemblance, not evidence about mechanism.

nodes.description:
The ordering claim of the entry, and a negative result carries most of it. In PKHD1L1-deficient mice the bundle develops normally: cohesion is undisturbed, tectorial-membrane attachment crowns form, stereocilin localises correctly to the tips of the tall row, the imprints of the bundle in the tectorial membrane are still present at six months, and planar cell polarity is normal. Mechanotransduction is intact too - FM1-43, which enters hair cells through open transduction channels, loads normally. Only afterwards, from about six weeks of age, does the bundle begin to fail. The disease is therefore a failure to maintain a correctly built bundle, not a failure to build one.
The expression time course sharpens what "maintain" can mean here, and it is worth being precise. PKHD1L1 protein is present on the bundle only in the first ten postnatal days, is largely gone by day 10 and is completely cleared from mature hair cells by day 21 - three weeks before the bundle starts to fail. The protein is therefore not present to perform ongoing maintenance. What its presence during development must be setting is the durability of the finished bundle, which is how the authors themselves put it: expression during development establishes bundles robust enough to last.

nodes.description: The model that carries nearly all of the mechanism in this entry. Deleting Pkhd1l1 in hair cells removes the stereocilia surface coat at the tips while leaving development, mechanotransduction and tectorial-membrane attachment intact, and produces progressive hearing loss beginning at high frequencies. The same line, followed for longer in a second study, gives the bundle-maintenance and noise-susceptibility results; a constitutive knockout made subsequently reproduces the hearing phenotype, which addresses the possibility that the Atoh1-Cre transgene rather than the deletion drives it.

Hearing aids are the reported management. The proband of Family 2, whose loss is moderate to severe, uses them bilaterally; nothing else is reported for any of the four patients. Amplification does not act on the mechanism - it raises the signal reaching a cochlea whose amplifier is failing.

nodes.description: PKHD1L1 is the first identified molecular component of the electron-dense surface coat on hair-cell stereocilia. Immunogold electron microscopy puts it towards the stereocilia tips, at highest density in the top 300 nanometres, in all three rows and preferentially in the high-frequency base of the cochlea. Mice lacking it in hair cells lose the coat at the upper part of the stereocilia while the coat at the bases is unaffected - so the coat is not one substance, and PKHD1L1 accounts for the upper portion of it.

nodes.description: Distortion product otoacoustic emissions are the direct readout of outer hair cell function, and they fail. In the mouse, DPOAE thresholds are elevated from three weeks in the high-frequency region and progress with age. In humans, the proband of the Chinese family had absent DPOAEs with normal tympanograms, which the authors read as outer hair cell dysfunction. Because mechanotransduction is intact in the mutant, this is a failure of the amplifier through a degrading bundle rather than a failure of the transduction apparatus.

nodes.description: Two damaged copies of PKHD1L1, which encodes a 4243-amino-acid protein that is almost entirely extracellular - a large ectodomain of IPT repeats, a single transmembrane helix, and a cytoplasmic tail of only a handful of residues. The reported human alleles span the mutation classes: a nonsense variant p.(Arg3381Ter) predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay, a frameshift p.(Leu2818TyrfsTer5), a variant annotated as missense, p.(Gly605Arg), that a minigene assay shows is really a splice allele causing exon 17 skipping, and two missense alleles whose recombinant protein fragments are measurably destabilised.

nodes.description: A noise dose calibrated to cause only a temporary threshold shift in wild-type mice causes a permanent one in PKHD1L1-deficient mice. Control thresholds recover to baseline by two weeks; mutant thresholds do not, at two weeks or at eight. Morphologically the difference shows as tall-row stereocilia loss and disorganisation after noise, on top of the short-row loss that ageing alone produces. The bundle that develops without a coat is therefore not just slower to fail with age - it is less able to absorb an acoustic insult.

nodes.description: Zebrafish carry two pkhd1l1 paralogues, and knocking out both gives auditory impairment that is already present in the larva. The line matters here for one specific reason: its time course resembles the human disease more closely than the mouse's does, which is what makes the mouse-human onset difference a species question rather than a curation error.
